title: Title: what you actually own, and what sits on top of it
summary: Title is the bundle of legal rights you hold in land, and the form of ownership decides what you can do with it and who inherits it. Every parcel also carries encumbrances, such as mortgages, easements and covenants, that belong to someone else or limit your use. Before you price land, you must know exactly what you are buying and what comes with it.
body:
Mr Shabazz, when you buy land you are not buying dirt. You are buying a bundle of legal rights, in a particular form of ownership, with other people’s rights already sitting on top of it. Title is the record of that bundle, and if you have not read it, you do not know what you own.

Recall

Q. From asset types, what is RevPAR?

A. Revenue per available room: rooms revenue divided by room nights available, which equals average daily rate times occupancy.

Q. From feasibility, what is a capture rate?

A. The share of all qualifying demand in a market that a project must win to meet its own schedule.

Q. From how tax works, why does the line between income and capital matter?

A. Because many systems tax business income and capital gains differently, so whether a sale is part of a trade or the disposal of an investment can change the tax result. The tests are fact-based and vary by country; verify against the primary source.

Why this matters

LEX here. A developer’s whole business plan sits on one assumption: that the land can be used, built on, financed and sold as intended. Title decides whether that is true. A drainage easement can remove a fifth of the buildable area. A restrictive covenant can forbid the use you planned. A form of co-ownership can hand a partner’s share to a stranger. These are found by reading, cheaply, before the deposit goes hard, or by litigation, expensively, afterwards.

Forms of ownership

In plain English, the strongest form of ownership in common law systems is what lawyers call fee simple, or freehold: ownership of land with no fixed end, which you can sell, mortgage and leave to your heirs. A leasehold is the right to occupy and use land for a fixed term under a lease, after which it returns to the owner. A condominium, called strata title in some places, divides a building into individually owned units and shared common elements. And when two or more people own the same land together, the form of co-ownership matters: under a joint tenancy, when one owner dies their share passes automatically to the survivors; under a tenancy in common, each owner holds a distinct share that passes under their own will.

The professional framing is that each form is a different set of rights against the world, and each lender, buyer and tax authority treats them differently. Civil law systems, such as Quebec’s, use their own terms and structures for the same ideas, so the labels do not travel across borders.

Worked example one, hypothetical. Two partners buy a site together for $2,000,000, each contributing $1,000,000, and their lawyer registers them as joint tenants because it is the default on the form. Three years later one partner dies. Under a joint tenancy, the survivor now owns the whole site and the deceased partner’s family receives nothing from it, whatever his will says. Had they registered as tenants in common, each holding half, the deceased partner’s half would have passed under his will. One box on a transfer form moved $1,000,000 of value. Whether survivorship applies, and how a co-ownership is created, depends on the law of the place; verify against the primary source.

Say that out loud now.

Encumbrances: other people’s rights in your land

An encumbrance is any right or interest in land held by someone other than the owner, or any limit on the owner’s use. Common examples are mortgages and other security, liens for unpaid work or taxes, leases, restrictive covenants that limit what can be built or how land is used, and easements. An easement is a right to use part of someone else’s land for a specific purpose, such as a right of way, a drainage pipe or a utility line. Many easements run with the land: they bind every future owner, including you, whether or not you knew about them when you bought.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A site is 40 metres wide and 50 metres deep, 2,000 square metres. Title shows a registered drainage easement 6 metres wide running the full depth along one side, 300 square metres, on which no permanent structure may be built. If the zoning allows a building footprint of 60 percent of the site, the planned footprint was 1,200 square metres. With the easement, the buildable part is 1,700 square metres, and the footprint must fit within it and its setbacks. If the setbacks and the easement together cut the footprint to 1,000 square metres, you have lost about 17 percent of every floor. The seller’s price was set for the full site.

Title insurance and condominium declarations, in brief

Title insurance is an insurance policy that protects an owner or a lender against loss from defects in title that existed at the date of the policy and were not excluded. It is common in some markets and less used in others. A condominium declaration is the registered document that creates a condominium and sets out the units, the common elements and each owner’s share of costs and votes. Both appear later this week. For today, note that both are read against the title itself: the policy lists what it will not cover, and the declaration lists the rights and duties every owner inherits.

Leasehold land: a clock on the value

Some sites are offered not for sale but on a long ground lease, under which you build on land you will never own and hand the building back at the end. Worked example three, hypothetical: a 99-year ground lease has 60 years left. A lender offering a 25-year amortising loan will usually want the lease to run well beyond the loan, so 60 years may be acceptable. A buyer in 30 years’ time, however, is buying a building with 30 years of life left in the lease, and will price it as a wasting asset whose value falls toward zero as the end approaches. A leasehold is not worse than freehold, but it is a different product with a clock running on it, and the clock belongs in your exit assumptions from the first day. The terms that matter most are the length, the rent and how it is reviewed, and what happens to the building at expiry; each is negotiated, not standard.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pricing land before reading its title. The control: obtain a title search and a current survey before the deposit becomes non-refundable, have counsel report every encumbrance in writing with its effect on your plan, and make satisfactory title a condition of the purchase.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner reads the owner’s name on the title and stops. The professional reads every registered instrument, asks what each one does to the plan, and asks what might affect the land without being on the register at all.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the form of ownership can affect who is taxed on a sale and how a transfer between owners is treated; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: an owner can inherit duties under easements and covenants, such as maintaining a shared drain. Banking: a lender takes security over title and will insist that its mortgage ranks first and that title is insurable. Governance: co-owners need a written agreement on decisions, because the register says who owns, not who decides. Estate: joint tenancy and tenancy in common pass differently on death, so the form must match the estate plan. Exit: every encumbrance you accept, a buyer will also inherit, and price.

Callback

In Week 20 you learned that a contract binds the parties who make it. A registered easement or covenant goes further: it binds people who never signed it, including every future owner. And in Week 8 you met the will and powers of attorney; today showed how a co-ownership form can quietly override a will.

Recap

Title is the bundle of rights you hold, in a form of ownership that decides what you can do and who inherits. Every parcel carries encumbrances, such as mortgages, liens, covenants and easements, many of which bind every future owner. Read the title and survey before you price the land.

Next: Ford, Failure Forensics — Champlain Towers South, and what a condominium’s ownership structure did to the repair of a shared building.
checklist: Obtain a title search and a current survey before any deposit goes hard.
Make satisfactory title a written condition of the purchase.
Have counsel report every registered instrument and its effect on the plan.
Plot every easement and covenant on the site plan before design starts.
Choose the co-ownership form deliberately and match it to each owner’s estate plan.
Ask what could affect the land without appearing on the register.
Record every encumbrance a buyer will inherit at exit.

speak: Title is the bundle of legal rights I hold in land, in a particular form of ownership. Fee simple, or freehold, is ownership with no end date. A leasehold is a right for a fixed term. A condominium divides a building into units and common elements. And co-ownership matters: under a joint tenancy, a share passes to the survivors on death; under a tenancy in common, it passes under each owner’s will. On hypothetical numbers, two partners each putting in a million can see a million move to the survivor because of one box on a form. Every parcel also carries encumbrances: mortgages, liens, covenants and easements, which are rights to use part of my land for a purpose, and many bind every future owner. terms: Fee simple — the fullest form of land ownership in common law systems, with no fixed end, transferable and inheritable.
Encumbrance — any right or interest in land held by someone other than the owner, or any limit on the owner’s use.
Easement — a right to use part of another person’s land for a specific purpose, such as access or drainage, often binding future owners.

hostile.q: Your site plan uses the full width of the lot. Have you checked the title for easements?
hostile.a: Yes. The search shows a 6-metre drainage easement along the east side, which is plotted on the plan, and the footprint has been redrawn to sit outside it. Counsel’s report lists every registered instrument with its effect, and good title is a condition of our purchase.

role: Failure forensics, with Cole assisting on legal matters
title: Champlain Towers South 2021: a shared structure and nobody’s urgency
summary: On 24 June 2021, part of Champlain Towers South, a twelve-storey condominium in Surfside, Florida, collapsed, and 98 people died. A 2018 engineering report had described major structural damage below the pool deck; repairs were debated for years, and a large special assessment was approved only in 2021. The technical cause is for the investigators; the governance lesson is that the ownership form left urgent work to an under-funded owners’ board.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this is the most serious case in this course so far, and it must be read with care. Ninety-eight people died. The technical cause of the collapse is a matter for the official investigation. What this lesson studies is narrower: how the ownership structure of a condominium left the repair of a shared structure to a volunteer board, with too little money, for too long.

Recall

Q. From this week, what is an easement?

A. A right to use part of another person’s land for a specific purpose, such as access or drainage, which often binds every future owner.

Q. From feasibility, what is Rule 28?

A. Count only end-user demand as absorption; track the investor share of every pre-sale, and never fund a long build with money that comes due before the building can pay it back.

Q. From how tax works, what is a flow-through entity?

A. An entity whose income is taxed in the hands of its owners rather than at the entity level, such as many partnerships.

Why this matters

Ford here, with Cole assisting on the legal side. A developer who builds condominiums creates a governance structure that outlives him: a declaration, an owners’ corporation, a budget and a reserve. He also often sells into, or buys within, existing condominiums. This case shows what happens when that structure cannot turn a known problem into money and repairs in time. This lesson relies on the broad public record. The federal investigation into the technical cause had not reached its final conclusions in the sources this lesson relies on; do not treat any single technical cause as established.

Step 1: Timeline

Champlain Towers South was a twelve-storey residential condominium in Surfside, Florida, completed in the early 1980s and governed by a condominium association of unit owners. In 2018, an engineering firm hired by the association reported major structural damage to the concrete slab below the pool deck and entrance drive, linked to failed waterproofing, along with cracking and deterioration in parts of the garage, and recommended repairs. The building was approaching a forty-year safety recertification required locally. Over the following years, the scope and cost of repairs were debated, board membership changed and estimated costs rose. In 2021 the association approved a special assessment of roughly $15 million, and a letter to owners that spring warned that the deterioration had accelerated. Repair work had not substantially begun when, in the early hours of 24 June 2021, a large part of the building collapsed. Ninety-eight people died. In 2022, Florida enacted legislation requiring periodic structural inspections and reserve studies for many older condominium buildings; verify the current requirements against the primary source.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three kinds of decision mattered. How the original declaration and budget set up the reserve for major repairs. How the board responded to the 2018 report: what was approved, when, and how it was funded. And how the owners, who vote on assessments, weighed the cost of repair against their own budgets.

Step 3: Assumptions

The working assumption, common in many associations, was that a building that is standing is safe for now, and that repairs could be scheduled and funded over time. A second assumption was that an engineering report describing serious damage set out a maintenance problem rather than an urgent one. A third was that reserves and assessments could be raised when needed.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Incentives

In a condominium, the people who must pay for a major repair are the same people who vote on it, and the cost lands on each household at once. Owners on fixed incomes or with little equity face real hardship. Board members are usually volunteers without engineering training. Low monthly fees help unit sales, which can push a developer, at the start, to set a modest reserve contribution. No one in that structure is paid to insist on the expensive answer early.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The 2018 report itself was the clearest sign. Rising cost estimates were another, because deterioration that is getting more expensive to fix is deterioration that is progressing. The approach of the recertification deadline was a third. The 2021 letter to owners shows that the seriousness was understood before the collapse.

Step 6: Point of no return

For the purposes of this lesson, which studies governance and not engineering, the decisive window was the period after the 2018 report, when work could have been scoped, funded and started. Each year of delay raised the cost and, according to the association’s own later warnings, worsened the condition.

Step 7: Root cause

Cole’s summary on the governance side: the ownership form placed responsibility for a shared structure on a volunteer board, funded by owners who voted on their own bills, with reserves that were not sized to the building’s real repair needs. Known, documented deterioration therefore waited for money and consensus. The technical causes of the collapse are for the investigators; the failure to turn a known structural warning into funded work promptly is the lesson for anyone who designs or buys into a condominium.

What a developer controls

Cole again. A developer writing a declaration and a first-year budget has more influence over the next forty years than any later board. He can commission a reserve study before the first budget, set contributions to fund major components over their real lives, require periodic structural inspections in the governing documents where the law allows, and give the board clear authority to act on an engineer’s urgent recommendation. A buyer of a condominium unit or building can ask for the last structural reports, the reserve study and the board minutes before signing. These are cheap acts with long consequences. Professional sign-off required: a structural engineer for any assessment of building condition, and a condominium lawyer for the governing documents.

The small-developer version

This is a composite example. A developer buys a 30-unit older condominium building to renovate and resell some units, and finds that the reserve fund is a fraction of what a reserve study says the roof and balconies will need within five years. The board has deferred the work for years to keep fees down. The developer now owns many votes, and so many of the bills. If he treats the reserve shortfall as someone else’s problem, the work keeps waiting and the building’s condition keeps worsening. If he treats it as part of the purchase price, he can negotiate the price down, fund the reserve and lead the board to commission the repairs on a date. The structure is the same as the case at a fraction of the scale; the difference is whether a warning becomes an instruction with a date.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating a structural engineering report as an item for discussion rather than an instruction with a date. The control: every structural finding gets a written response with a funded plan and a start date, and reserves are set from a professional reserve study, not from what keeps fees low.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner buying into a condominium reads the unit and the monthly fee. The professional reads the reserve study, the last two structural reports and the minutes of every board meeting where they were discussed.

Callback

In Week 21 you studied negligence and the duty of care; the many claims that followed this collapse turned on who owed what duty to whom. And in Week 2 you learned the pre-mortem: imagine the failure and ask why. Run one on any shared building and the first question becomes who has the authority, and the money, to act on bad news.

Recap

A condominium association received a report of major structural damage in 2018, debated and delayed costly repairs, and approved a large assessment in 2021. The building partly collapsed that June and 98 people died. The technical cause is for the investigators; the governance failure is plain. Rule 30 follows from it.

Rule 30: Before I build, buy into or sell a shared structure, I read who is legally responsible for repairing it, how the repair money is reserved, and what has been reported but not fixed, and I treat every structural warning as an instruction with a date.

Next: Roman, The Money — what title defects, easements and under-funded reserves cost, and what title insurance does about it.
checklist: Commission a reserve study before setting any condominium’s first budget.
Set reserve contributions to fund major components over their real lives.
Give the board clear authority to act on an engineer’s urgent recommendation.
Request the last structural reports, the reserve study and board minutes before buying into a condominium.
Give every structural finding a written response, a funded plan and a start date.
Get a structural engineer’s sign-off on building condition and a condominium lawyer on the governing documents.
Run the seven steps on any building failure you study.

speak: Champlain Towers South was a twelve-storey condominium in Surfside, Florida, governed by its unit owners’ association. In 2018 an engineer it hired reported major structural damage below the pool deck and recommended repairs. For years the work was debated, costs rose and boards changed. In 2021 owners approved a special assessment of roughly 15 million dollars, and a letter that spring warned the damage was getting worse. On 24 June 2021 much of the building collapsed and 98 people died. The technical cause is for the official investigators. The governance lesson is clear: a volunteer board, funded by owners voting on their own bills, with reserves too small for the building’s real needs, could not turn a known warning into funded work in time. terms: Condominium association — the body of unit owners that governs a condominium, maintains common elements and sets fees.
Special assessment — a one-time charge levied on unit owners to pay for a cost the regular budget and reserves cannot cover.
Reserve study — a professional estimate of a building’s major components, their remaining lives and replacement costs, used to set reserve contributions.

hostile.q: You are selling units in this building. Why should a buyer trust that the structure has been maintained?
hostile.a: Because we give them the evidence before they sign: the last two structural reports, the reserve study, the funding plan for every finding and the board minutes approving it. Where a report recommends work, the plan shows the date it starts and the money that pays for it.

title: What title problems cost, and what title insurance does about it
summary: Title problems reach your money three ways: they cut what you can build, they block or delay financing and sale, and in condominiums they surface as special assessments. Title insurance transfers the cost of some hidden defects for a one-time premium, but it excludes what is known, what a survey would show and many off-title risks. Price each problem into the land, the reserve or the decision to walk.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a title problem is a money problem in legal clothing. It cuts what you can build, it delays the loan and the sale, and in a condominium it arrives as a bill to every owner. Title insurance helps with some of this and not with the rest, and the difference matters.

Recall

Q. From this week, what was the governance lesson of Champlain Towers South?

A. That a volunteer board funded by owners voting on their own bills, with reserves too small for the building’s needs, could not turn a known structural warning into funded work in time.

Q. From feasibility, what is the fair share test?

A. Compare your required capture rate with your units divided by all competing new units in the window; required capture above fair share means you must be better or cheaper.

Q. From how tax works, what does residence-based taxation reach?

A. Often the worldwide income of a resident taxpayer, subject to credits and treaties for tax paid elsewhere; verify against the primary source.

Why this matters

Roman here. Lenders will not fund against title they cannot rely on, and buyers will not pay full price for land with a cloud on it. So title is not a closing formality; it is part of the value. If you can put a number on each title problem, you can decide whether to price it, insure it, reserve for it or walk away.

Channel one: lost buildable value

In plain English, an easement or covenant that limits where or what you can build removes value directly. The professional framing is to price it through the residual land value: what the land is worth after the finished project’s value pays for construction, costs and the developer’s required profit.

Worked example one, with hypothetical numbers. On a clean site, a 100-unit project supports a residual land value of $4,000,000, about $40,000 per unit. Title reveals a covenant limiting height that cuts the project to 85 units. If the residual per unit stays roughly the same, land value falls to about $3,400,000. In practice it often falls further, because some costs, such as the site work and the lift cores, do not shrink with the unit count. If the seller’s price was set for 100 units, you either renegotiate about $600,000 or more off the price, or you are paying for units you cannot build.

Channel two: time, financing and sale

A defect that must be cleared before closing, such as an old mortgage not formally discharged or a lien for unpaid work, delays the loan. Each month of delay carries interest and holding costs. On a hypothetical $10,000,000 acquisition loan at 8 percent, a three-month delay costs about $200,000 of interest. A buyer at exit will ask the same questions, so an unresolved defect also sits on your sale price.

Channel three: special assessments in condominiums

Worked example two, hypothetical. A 100-unit condominium building needs $10,000,000 of structural and envelope repairs. Its reserve fund holds $2,000,000. The shortfall of $8,000,000 is levied as a special assessment, on average $80,000 per unit. A buyer looking at a unit priced at $400,000 should treat it as costing about $480,000 if the assessment is coming, and a lender will ask whether the owner can pay it. Units in under-reserved buildings often trade at a discount for exactly this reason. For a developer buying an existing condominium building to reposition, the reserve shortfall is part of the price.

Say that out loud now.

What title insurance does, and does not do

Title insurance is a policy, usually paid for with a one-time premium at closing, that protects an owner or lender against loss from title defects that existed at the policy date and are not excluded. The professional framing is to read the exceptions first, because the policy’s value lies in what remains after them. Policies commonly exclude defects you knew about, matters a current survey would have shown, defects created after the policy date and many government regulations such as zoning. Premiums and coverage vary by market and insurer; treat any figure here as illustrative. Worked example three, hypothetical: on a $20,000,000 acquisition, a premium of $40,000 might insure against an unknown defect that, if it arose, could cost $1,000,000 to cure. It cannot insure the drainage easement you already found, because that is now known.

How the best do it

Experienced institutional buyers typically order the title report, the survey and a zoning review together, early, and compare all three: every survey feature is checked against a title instrument, every instrument is plotted on the survey, and the zoning review confirms what the remaining land can legally support. What a small developer can copy is the overlay: one site plan with every easement, covenant and survey finding drawn on it, reviewed before the deposit goes hard.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick’s note. On your personal balance sheet, record land at a value that reflects its title, not the asking price. If you own condominium units, note the reserve position of each building, because an assessment is a future liability that never appears on your statement until it is levied. And record how each property is held, jointly or in common, because that decides what passes under your will.

Working with advisers

This month’s thread. Title is where three advisers must work together: the lawyer who reads the title, the surveyor who maps the land and the title insurer who decides what to cover. Problems hide in the gaps between them. Instruct them to talk to each other, give each the others’ reports and ask your lawyer for one consolidated memo.

Then challenge the memo. Ask, for each encumbrance, what it does to the plan, who it benefits, whether it can be released, and whether the policy covers it. An adviser who answers those four questions for every line is doing the work you are paying for.

Worked example four: price, insure, reserve or walk

All figures are hypothetical. A site’s title review produces four findings. A height covenant costs 15 units, about $600,000 of land value: you price it, by renegotiating the purchase price. An old undischarged mortgage from a lender that no longer exists will take time to clear: you reserve for it, holding back $100,000 at closing until the discharge arrives. A possible gap in the chain of title fifty years ago cannot be resolved by search: you insure it, by asking the insurer to cover it without exception. And a right of way across the middle of the site that the neighbour refuses to release: you walk, because no design works around it and your kill criteria said so.

Four findings, four different tools. The mistake is using one tool for everything: insuring what you could have priced, or negotiating for months over a problem that should have ended the deal on the first day.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming title insurance makes title problems go away. The control: price known problems into the land or walk, insure only the unknown, and read the policy exceptions before closing.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner orders title insurance and skips the survey to save money. Many policies then exclude exactly what the survey would have found.

Callback

In Week 13 you met contingency for unknown costs. Title risk splits the same way: known problems go into the price, unknown ones go to insurance or contingency. In Week 28, feasibility taught you to write kill criteria; a title problem that cuts the unit count below your criteria is a reason to walk, not to negotiate.

Recap

Title problems cost buildable value, time and, in condominiums, special assessments. Title insurance covers some unknown defects for a one-time premium and excludes what is known or surveyable. Price, insure, reserve or walk, and record each property’s title position on your own balance sheet.

Next: Vera, The Rules — how title is proved: registers, searches, priority and the risks that never appear on title.
checklist: Price every title limitation through the residual land value.
Estimate the interest cost of any closing delay caused by a defect.
Calculate the reserve shortfall per unit before buying into a condominium.
Read title insurance exceptions before relying on the policy.
Order title report, survey and zoning review together and overlay them.
Get one consolidated memo from your title lawyer covering every encumbrance.
Record land at a title-adjusted value and note each condominium’s reserve position.

Policy exception — a matter a title insurance policy expressly does not cover.

hostile.q: You have a title policy. Why do you also need a survey?
hostile.a: Because the policy excludes matters a current survey would have shown, such as encroachments and boundary issues, unless we provide one. The survey also lets us plot every easement against the design. Without it, the policy covers less and we know less.

title: How title is proved: registers, searches and the risks off the record
summary: Title is proved through a public register, but registers work in two different ways: some record documents and leave you to prove the chain, others record title itself and back it with the state. Priority usually follows the order of registration. Some rights bind land without appearing on title, so a search is never the whole diligence.
body:
Mr Shabazz, title is only as good as the evidence behind it. Some registers record documents and leave you to prove the chain; others record title itself and stand behind it. Either way, some rights bind land without ever appearing on the register, so the search is where diligence starts, not where it ends.

Recall

Q. From this week, what does title insurance commonly exclude?

A. Defects you knew about, matters a current survey would show, defects created after the policy date and many government regulations such as zoning.

Q. From feasibility, what are kill criteria?

A. Specific results, written and dated before the land money goes hard, that stop the project at a go/no-go gate.

Q. From how tax works, what is source-based taxation?

A. Taxation by the country where income arises, such as where a building sits, regardless of where the owner lives.

Why this matters

Vera here. A developer usually relies on a lawyer’s title report, and should. But knowing how the report is built lets you ask the right questions: how far back the search went, what the register guarantees, what was checked off the register, and what the lawyer could not verify. Title disputes are won and lost on records, and you should know which records you have.

Two kinds of register

In plain English, there are two broad approaches. In a deeds or registry system, the public office keeps copies of documents affecting land, such as transfers, mortgages and easements, in the order they were registered. The register does not say who owns the land. A lawyer reads the documents back through time, the chain of title, to show that each transfer was valid and that nothing undischarged remains. In a title registration system, often called a Torrens system after the reformer associated with it, the register itself states who owns the land and what interests affect it, and the state generally stands behind that statement, often with a compensation fund for people who lose out through registry error.

The professional framing is that the first system makes you prove title, while the second gives you title by registration, subject to exceptions set by statute. In both, the details, such as how far back a search must go and what the state guarantees, are set by local law. Many places use a mix, with older parcels in one system and newer ones in the other, or a programme to convert. Verify against the primary source for the jurisdiction of each parcel.

Worked example one, hypothetical. In a registry system, a lawyer searches the documents for a parcel over a statutory period, say forty years, and finds a mortgage registered thirty years ago with no discharge recorded. The lender that granted it was merged into another bank twenty years ago. Before closing, someone must obtain a discharge from the successor bank or prove the debt was repaid. That takes weeks, and the purchase agreement should say who pays and what happens if it cannot be done. In a title registration system, the same old mortgage would appear on the current register, which makes it easier to find but no easier to remove.

Say that out loud now.

Priority: who ranks first

When two people have conflicting interests in the same land, the law needs a rule for who wins. In many systems, the general rule is that interests registered earlier rank ahead of those registered later, subject to exceptions such as notice or fraud. That is why lenders insist their mortgage be registered at closing and searched again immediately before funding, a step often called a subsearch or bring-down. Priority rules and their exceptions vary by jurisdiction; verify against the primary source.

Worked example two, hypothetical. You agree to buy a site and your lender agrees to fund on Tuesday. On Monday, a contractor who worked for the seller registers a lien for $150,000 of unpaid work. If your lender funds without searching again, its mortgage may rank behind the lien, and you may take title subject to it. If the bring-down search catches it, the seller must pay it off, or you hold back $150,000 from the price until it is discharged. One search, run on the morning of closing, decides who carries $150,000.

Risks off the register

Some rights can bind land without appearing on title. Depending on the jurisdiction, these may include certain short leases, rights of people in actual occupation, claims to ownership by long possession, unpaid property taxes or utility charges, municipal work orders and outstanding building permits, and rights arising from the way land has been used, such as a long-standing path across it. A lawyer’s title report usually lists what was searched off the register, such as tax and municipal searches, and what was not. Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer qualified in the jurisdiction for the title opinion, and a land surveyor for the survey.

Keeping the evidence

Keep a title file for every property: the search, the survey, the opinion, every registered instrument and every letter about discharges and releases. If a dispute arises years later, the file is the evidence. Store it so that someone other than you, such as an executor or a buyer’s lawyer, could find and read it.

Rights that grow from use

Two kinds of off-register right deserve special care because they are created by behaviour over time rather than by a document. In some jurisdictions, a person who openly occupies land for a long statutory period, without permission, may acquire ownership of it, a doctrine often called adverse possession. And a long-standing use of a path or drain across land may, in some places, give rise to an easement even though nothing was ever signed or registered. Whether either can happen, and on what conditions, varies by jurisdiction, and title registration systems often restrict them; verify against the primary source.

The practical defence is the survey and a site visit. A fence that does not follow the boundary, a neighbour’s shed over the line, a worn footpath across the site or a pipe outfall onto it are each a clue. Worked example three, hypothetical: the survey shows the neighbour’s fence sits 2 metres inside your boundary along 40 metres of frontage, 80 square metres. If the law of the place allows a possessory claim after a long period and the fence has stood that long, those 80 square metres may no longer be yours to build on, and your setback is now measured from the wrong line.

What to ask for in a title opinion

A useful title opinion states the registered owner, how the land is held, every registered instrument with its effect, the searches made off the register and their results, the date and scope of the search, what the lawyer did not check, and any qualifications. Ask for it in that order, in writing, and keep it in the title file.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating a clean search as clean title. The control: ask your lawyer in writing what the register guarantees in that jurisdiction, what was searched off the register, what was not, and whether a bring-down search will be run immediately before funding.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner assumes the register in one country works like the register in another. Each system has its own guarantees, search periods and exceptions, and the same word can mean different things.

Callback

In Week 19 you separated sources of law; land registration is one of the clearest places where statute, not case law, does most of the work. And in Week 25 you learned to instruct advisers in writing; a title instruction should ask the four questions in the biggest risk above, by name.

Recap

Registry systems record documents and make you prove the chain; title registration systems record title and usually stand behind it. Priority generally follows the order of registration, which is why the bring-down search matters. Some rights bind land without appearing on title, so ask what was searched off the register.

Next: Sage, The Numbers — reverse engineering what a title limitation is worth, and what a reserve fund must collect.
checklist: Confirm which registration system applies to each parcel.
Ask in writing what the register guarantees in that jurisdiction.
Ask how far back the search went and what was searched off the register.
Require a bring-down search immediately before funding.
Agree in the purchase contract who pays to clear old instruments, and what happens if they cannot be cleared.
Hold back part of the price for any defect not cleared at closing.
Keep a complete title file for every property that someone else could read.
head: Field checklist
speak: Title is proved through a register, and registers work in two ways. A registry system records documents in order, and a lawyer reads the chain back through time to prove each transfer and find anything undischarged. A title registration system, often called Torrens, records the title itself, and the state generally stands behind it. Either way, priority usually follows the order of registration. On hypothetical numbers, if a contractor registers a 150,000 lien the day before my lender funds, a bring-down search that morning decides whether the seller pays it or I inherit it. Some rights never appear on title at all: certain leases, occupiers’ rights, long possession, unpaid taxes and municipal orders. So I ask my lawyer in writing what the register guarantees, what was searched off it, what was not, and whether a bring-down search will run before funding, and I keep a title file someone else could read.
terms: Chain of title — the sequence of documents showing how ownership passed from owner to owner over time.
Torrens system — a land registration system in which the register states title and the state generally guarantees it.
Bring-down search — a final search of the register immediately before closing or funding, to catch anything registered since the last search.

hostile.q: Your title search is two weeks old. How do you know nothing has been registered since?
hostile.a: Because we do not fund on it. Our lawyer runs a bring-down search on the morning of closing, and the funding condition requires it to show nothing new. If something appears, the seller clears it or we hold back the amount from the price.

title: Reverse engineering: what a title release is worth, and what a reserve must collect
summary: Two calculations start from a finished outcome and work backward. First, the most you should pay a neighbour to release an easement, worked from the extra units it allows. Second, the monthly reserve contribution a condominium needs today to fund a known future repair. Both turn a title or governance question into a number you can negotiate with.
body:
Mr Shabazz, today we start at the finish line twice and work backward. First, from the extra building a released easement would allow, back to the most you should pay for the release. Second, from a repair a building will need in fifteen years, back to what each owner must put aside every month starting now.

Recall

Q. From this week, what is a bring-down search?

A. A final search of the register immediately before closing or funding, to catch anything registered since the last search.

Q. From feasibility, what does working backward from a sell-out date show?

A. The monthly pace and capture rate the financing really requires, which you can then compare with the market’s evidence.

Q. From how tax works, why might a payment to release an easement need tax advice?

A. Because how the payment is characterised, as part of the cost of land or as something else, can affect the tax treatment for both sides. Verify against the primary source before you rely on it.

Why this matters

Sage here. Title problems feel legal and abstract until someone puts a price on them. Neighbours who benefit from an easement will often release it for money, and condominium boards must decide how much to collect today for repairs that are years away. In both cases the honest number comes from working backward from the outcome. This is even-week reverse engineering.

Worked example one: the most you should pay for a release

All figures are hypothetical. Follow the units.

  1. The finished outcome. Without the easement, your design fits 104 units. With it, 90 units. The release is worth whatever 14 extra units are worth to you.
  2. Revenue per extra unit. Each unit sells for $400,000. Selling costs are 5 percent, $20,000. Net revenue per unit is $380,000.
  3. Cost per extra unit. Additional construction, soft and finance cost is $300,000 per unit. The extra units mostly add floor area, not new cores or site work, so this is a marginal cost, lower than the average.
  4. Margin per extra unit before land. $380,000 minus $300,000 is $80,000.
  5. Gross value of the release. 14 units times $80,000 is $1,120,000.
  6. Required profit on the extra work. You need a 15 percent profit on cost for taking the risk: 15 percent of 14 times $300,000, which is 15 percent of $4,200,000, or $630,000.
  7. Maximum price for the release. $1,120,000 minus $630,000 is $490,000. From that, deduct legal, survey and registration costs, say $40,000, and the cost of any delay. Your walk-away price is about $450,000.

Read it. Paying $300,000 for the release leaves you about $150,000 better off than not buying it, after your required profit. Paying $600,000 means you are giving away part of the return you need for the risk. The neighbour does not know your number, so do not tell them; but know it before you start talking.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: the reserve a future repair requires

  1. The finished outcome. A reserve study says the roof and façade of a 100-unit condominium must be replaced in 15 years, at an estimated cost of $3,000,000 in the money of that time.
  2. No interest, the simple case. $3,000,000 divided by 15 years is $200,000 a year. Divided by 100 units, $2,000 per unit a year, about $167 per unit a month.
  3. With interest earned on the reserve. If the fund earns 3 percent a year, less is needed each year, because contributions grow. The annual contribution is the target times the interest rate divided by the growth factor minus one. 1.03 to the power of 15 is about 1.558. So: $3,000,000 times 0.03 divided by 0.558, which is about $161,300 a year.
  4. Per unit. $161,300 divided by 100 units is about $1,613 a year, about $134 per unit a month.
  5. Start late and the bill grows. If the board delays five years and then funds the same $3,000,000 over the remaining 10 years at 3 percent, the annual contribution is $3,000,000 times 0.03 divided by about 0.344, which is about $261,700, roughly $218 per unit a month. Delay five years and the monthly bill rises by more than 60 percent.
  6. Delay until the year of the repair. The whole $3,000,000 arrives as a special assessment, $30,000 per unit at once.

Read it. The same repair costs $134 a month if planned from the start, $218 a month if planned five years late, and $30,000 in a single bill if not planned at all. This is the arithmetic behind the Champlain Towers lesson: delay does not avoid the cost, it concentrates it.

How to use both numbers

The release price is a negotiating ceiling, not an offer. Open well below it and stop at it. The reserve contribution is a design decision a developer makes in the first budget; setting it low to help sales hands the bigger number to the owners later. Professional sign-off required: a reserve study by a qualified professional, and a lawyer for the release and its registration.

Worked example three: what delay does to the release price

  1. The finished outcome. The neighbour agrees to release the easement, but registration and the redesign will delay the start of construction by six months.
  2. Carry during the delay. You hold a land loan of $3,000,000 at 8 percent: about $20,000 a month in interest. Add $5,000 a month of tax, insurance and site security. Six months is $150,000.
  3. Return lost to time. The whole project’s profit arrives six months later. On a hypothetical project profit of $4,000,000 and a 15 percent annual required return, six months of delay costs roughly half a year’s return on that profit, about $300,000 in present-value terms, as a rough estimate.
  4. Revised ceiling. The $450,000 walk-away price, less $150,000 of carry and about $300,000 of time cost, leaves about zero.
  5. Read it. With a six-month delay, the release is barely worth buying at any price. With a one-month delay, it is worth most of the $450,000. The neighbour’s price matters less than how fast the release can be signed and registered.

That changes the negotiation. Offer a higher price for a fast signature, with the release drafted by your lawyer and ready to register on the day it is signed, rather than a low price that invites months of back and forth.

A note on the rough estimate in step 3. The cost of delay depends on the project’s actual cash flows, and a full model would discount each one. The rough version is enough to show the shape: on a project with a large profit at the end, time is often worth more than the price of the thing you are waiting for.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is negotiating a release or a reserve without a number, so the result is set by the other side’s patience or by what feels affordable. The control: work backward from the outcome to a ceiling or a contribution, write it down and decide against it.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner values the release at the full margin on the extra units and forgets the profit he needs for the risk of building them. The professional prices the release at what is left after a required return.

Callback

In Week 17 you reverse engineered public deals to find an implied land price. The release calculation is the same tool applied to a slice of land. In Week 11 you learned the time value of money: the reserve fund’s interest is that idea working for the owners, and the late start is that idea working against them.

Recap

Work backward from 14 extra units to a release worth about $450,000 at most after a required profit and costs. Work backward from a $3,000,000 repair to about $134 per unit a month if started now, $218 if started five years late, or $30,000 at once if ignored. Know the number before you negotiate.

Next: LEX, The Room — the closing call where a surprise appears on title.
checklist: Measure the units or area an encumbrance costs in your actual design.
Use marginal cost per extra unit, not average cost, when valuing a release.
Deduct your required profit on the extra work before setting a ceiling.
Deduct legal, survey, registration and delay costs from the ceiling.
Calculate reserve contributions with and without interest earned.
Show the cost of a five-year delay in reserve funding.
Get a qualified reserve study before setting any first-year budget.
head: Field checklist
speak: I worked backward twice. First, a neighbour’s easement costs me 14 units. Each extra unit nets 380,000 after selling costs and costs 300,000 at the margin, so the units are worth 1.12 million. I need a 15 percent profit on the 4.2 million of extra cost, which is 630,000. That leaves 490,000, and after 40,000 of legal and survey costs, my walk-away price for the release is about 450,000. I open well below it and do not reveal it. Second, a condominium needs a 3 million roof and facade in 15 years. With the reserve earning 3 percent, it needs about 161,000 a year, about 134 dollars per unit a month. Start five years late and it is about 218 dollars a month. Ignore it and it is a 30,000 dollar special assessment per unit. Delay does not avoid the cost; it concentrates it.
terms: Release of easement — a registered document by which the holder of an easement gives it up, freeing the land from it.
Sinking fund — money set aside regularly, earning interest, to pay a known future cost.
Marginal cost — the extra cost of producing one more unit, as distinct from the average cost of all units.

hostile.q: The neighbour wants 700,000 to release the easement. Why not pay it and move on?
hostile.a: Because the 14 extra units are worth about 490,000 to us after the profit we need for building them, and about 450,000 after costs. At 700,000 we would be paying the neighbour more than the units earn us. Our ceiling is set; above it, we build the 90-unit scheme.

title: The closing call when something new appears on title
summary: On the morning of closing, the bring-down search shows a lien the seller says is a mistake and promises to fix after closing. The question behind the question is who carries the risk until it is fixed. Answer with a holdback, a written undertaking, an extension or a walk, never with trust alone.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the most dangerous sentence at a closing is “we’ll sort it out afterwards.” When something new appears on title on closing morning, the conversation is not about whether the seller is honest. It is about who carries the risk until the problem is gone, and in what form.

Recall

Q. From this week, what is the most you should pay to release an easement?

A. The value of the extra building it allows, after deducting the profit you need for the risk of building it and the costs of the release.

Q. From feasibility, why should the person testing demand not be the person who found the site?

A. Because the person who found the site wants it to work, and independence protects the test from that bias.

Q. From how tax works, why might the timing of a closing matter for tax?

A. Because many tax rules turn on the date of acquisition or disposal, such as which year income falls into; verify against the primary source.

Why this matters

LEX here. Closings happen under time pressure: the lender’s commitment expires, the seller has another deal, the deposit is at risk. That pressure is exactly when a surprise on title gets waved through. The habits in this lesson are what stop a $150,000 problem becoming yours because everyone wanted to finish by noon.

The scene

This is a composite example. You are closing on a development site for $5,000,000 at noon. At 9 in the morning, your lawyer calls: the bring-down search shows a construction lien registered two days ago by a landscaping contractor for $120,000, for work done for the seller. The seller’s lawyer says the claim is disputed, the contractor was paid in full, and the seller will have it removed within thirty days of closing. Your lender’s funding condition requires title free of liens. The seller says, “If we don’t close today, I have another buyer.”

The question behind the question

The seller is not really asking whether you trust him. He is asking whether you will carry the risk of his dispute, unpaid, until he gets round to fixing it. Once the money is paid, his incentive to fix it falls sharply. The real question is what form of protection replaces your leverage once you have paid.

Lines to say

  • “We can close today. We will hold back $150,000 from the price in our lawyer’s trust account until the lien is discharged, which covers the claim plus costs.”
  • “If you would rather not hold back, we need a written undertaking from your lawyer to discharge it within thirty days, and our lender will need to accept that.”
  • “Our lender cannot fund against an undischarged lien. That is their condition, not our preference.”
  • “If neither works, we can extend closing by a week while you clear it. I would rather close next Tuesday than inherit a dispute today.”

Say that out loud now.

The worked numbers behind your lines

All figures are hypothetical. The lien is $120,000. A holdback of $150,000 covers the claim and about $30,000 for interest, legal costs and the time to remove it. If you close without protection and the lien proves valid, you pay $120,000 plus your legal costs, perhaps $20,000, and your lender may treat the lien as a default on its loan. A week’s extension costs you, say, $10,000 in extra interest and fees. Against a possible $140,000 loss, the holdback or the extension is cheap.

Lines never to say

  • “That’s fine, we trust you.” Trust is not a form of security.
  • “We’ll take care of it ourselves.” You have just volunteered to pay someone else’s dispute.
  • “Let’s just close and sort out the details.” The lien is not a detail; it ranks against your title.
  • “Our lender won’t notice.” Your lender’s lawyer runs the same search.

When to stay silent

When the seller says he has another buyer, do not respond to it. A buyer who will close at noon over a fresh lien without protection is unlikely, and if one exists, you have learned something about the risk you were being asked to carry. Restate the holdback offer once, calmly, and wait.

If he pushes back

The seller may say the holdback is insulting, because the contractor was paid. Answer with the register, not with suspicion: “If the contractor was paid, the lien will come off quickly and the holdback comes back to you with it. The holdback costs you nothing if you are right.” That sentence lets the seller save face and still gives you protection. Make sure the holdback agreement in writing says who controls the money, what document releases it, and what happens if the lien is not discharged by a set date.

Holding your state

Closing-morning surprises trigger urgency. Slow your speech, ask your lawyer to read the registered document aloud, and write down the three options before you speak to the seller. A clear list of options sounds like control; an improvised answer sounds like panic. Professional sign-off required: your real estate lawyer on the holdback agreement and any undertaking, and your lender’s consent to the arrangement.

A second scenario: the tenant nobody mentioned

On the site visit the day before closing, you find a small business operating from a shed on the site. The seller says the tenant is “month to month” and will leave. Nothing appears on the register. Depending on the jurisdiction, a person in actual occupation, or a tenant under a short lease, may have rights that bind a buyer even though nothing is registered. Lines to say: “Before we close, we need the tenancy agreement, confirmation of the notice given and the date the tenant will leave. If they are still in occupation on closing day, we hold back an amount that covers the cost and time of ending the tenancy.” Lines never to say: “We’ll deal with them after we own it.” You have just bought the dispute and the seller’s goodwill with it.

After closing

Whatever was agreed, follow it to the end. Diary the date the lien must be discharged or the tenant must leave, ask your lawyer to confirm in writing when it happens, and release the holdback only against the document the agreement names. Record the episode in your decision journal: what appeared, what you offered, what it cost and how long it took. The next closing will be faster because of it, and you will know which of your advisers moved quickly when it mattered.

Then close the loop with the seller’s side as well. If the lien is discharged early, release the holdback promptly and say thank you in writing. You may want to buy from the same seller, or work with the same lawyers, again.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is closing over a new encumbrance on a promise. The control: no closing over anything new on title without a holdback, a lawyer’s written undertaking accepted by the lender, an extension or a decision to walk.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner treats the closing deadline as fixed and the title problem as negotiable. The professional treats the title as fixed and the deadline as negotiable.

Callback

In Week 6 you practised acknowledge, bridge, answer. Here: acknowledge the seller’s view of the dispute, bridge to the lender’s condition, answer with a holdback. In Week 27 you learned not to waive conditions on someone else’s deadline; closing over a lien is waiving a title condition under the same pressure.

Recap

When something new appears on title at closing, the question is who carries the risk until it is gone. Offer a holdback, a written undertaking accepted by the lender, an extension or a walk. Never close on trust, and never treat the deadline as more fixed than the title.

Next: Kema, Quiz & Recap — six questions on title, a Red Pen drill on a title report and the boardroom drill.
checklist: Require a bring-down search on the morning of closing.
Prepare holdback, undertaking and extension options before closing day.
Size any holdback to the claim plus interest, legal costs and time.
Confirm the lender accepts any undertaking or holdback before relying on it.
Put the holdback terms in writing: who holds it, what releases it, the deadline.
Ignore claims of another buyer and restate your offer once.
Never close over a new encumbrance on a promise alone.
head: Field checklist
speak: On closing morning the bring-down search shows a new 120,000-dollar lien from the seller’s contractor. The seller says it is disputed and promises to clear it within thirty days, and mentions another buyer. The question behind the question is who carries the risk until it is gone, because once I pay, his incentive to fix it falls. So I give three options. Close today with a 150,000 holdback in my lawyer’s trust account until the lien is discharged. Or a written undertaking from his lawyer that my lender accepts. Or a one-week extension while he clears it. If the lien is valid and I close without protection, it could cost me about 140,000 and trouble with my lender; the holdback costs him nothing if he is right. I never say we trust you, I ignore the other buyer, and I treat the title as fixed and the deadline as negotiable.
terms: Construction lien — a claim registered against land by someone who supplied work or materials to it and says they were not paid.
Holdback — part of the purchase price kept back, usually in a lawyer’s trust account, until a stated problem is resolved.
Undertaking — a formal written promise, often by a lawyer, that the profession treats as binding, to do a specified thing.

hostile.q: The seller’s lawyer has given an undertaking. Why are you still holding back money?
hostile.a: Because our lender’s funding condition requires either a discharged lien or security it accepts, and it has asked for the holdback. The undertaking is welcome and may shorten the time the money is held, but the holdback is what lets the lender fund today.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Title week: quiz, recap and the Red Pen
summary: Six questions test forms of ownership, easements, Rule 30, title insurance exceptions, registration systems and the closing holdback. The Red Pen drill finds the planted defects in a hypothetical title summary, and the boardroom drill explains title in two minutes.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week showed that land is a bundle of rights carrying other people’s rights, proved by records, insured only in part and, in a condominium, governed by owners who must fund what the building needs. Today you test it, then mark up a title summary that skipped half of it.

Recall

Q. From this week, what is the beginner’s mistake at a closing with a new lien?

A. Treating the deadline as fixed and the title problem as negotiable. The professional treats the title as fixed and the deadline as negotiable.

Q. From feasibility, why is a fast early sales start not proof of demand?

A. Because fast sales can come from speculation as well as genuine need; you must know who is buying and why.

Q. From how tax works, what is the difference between avoidance and evasion?

A. Avoidance arranges affairs within the law and discloses the facts; evasion hides or misstates facts and is a crime.

The six questions

Question 1. What is the difference between a joint tenancy and a tenancy in common? Answer: Under a joint tenancy, a co-owner’s share passes automatically to the survivors on death; under a tenancy in common, each owner’s distinct share passes under their own will. The law of the place decides how each is created.

Question 2. A 6-metre easement runs the depth of a 50-metre site. How much land does it remove from building, and why does it matter? Answer: 300 square metres, which can cut the building footprint and every floor above it, and many easements bind every future owner.

Question 3. What was the governance lesson of Champlain Towers South, and what is Rule 30? Answer: A volunteer board, funded by owners voting on their own bills, with inadequate reserves, could not turn a known structural warning into funded work in time. Rule 30: before I build, buy into or sell a shared structure, I read who is legally responsible for repairing it, how the repair money is reserved, and what has been reported but not fixed, and I treat every structural warning as an instruction with a date.

Question 4. Name three things title insurance commonly does not cover. Answer: Defects you already knew about, matters a current survey would have shown, and many government regulations such as zoning, as well as defects created after the policy date.

Question 5. How does a registry system differ from a title registration system? Answer: A registry system records documents and you prove title through the chain; a title registration system records the title itself, and the state generally stands behind it.

Question 6. A new $120,000 lien appears on closing morning. What are your options? Answer: A holdback sized to the claim and costs, a lawyer’s written undertaking accepted by the lender, an extension while the seller clears it, or walking away. Never close over it on a promise.

Recap

Title is the bundle of rights you hold, in a form of ownership that decides what you can do and who inherits. Encumbrances, especially easements and covenants, can cut what you can build and bind every future owner. Title problems cost value, time and, in condominiums, special assessments. Registers work in two ways, priority follows registration, and some rights never appear on title. Work backward to price a release or a reserve, and never close on a promise.

Say that out loud now.

Red Pen

Read this hypothetical extract from a title summary prepared for a purchase and find the defects before reading the list.

Title summary, hypothetical. Registered owners: A and B, as joint tenants. Encumbrances: a mortgage to a bank, to be discharged at closing; a utility easement, minor. Title insurance has been ordered, so no survey is required. Search completed three weeks ago; no further search needed. Buyer to take title as joint tenants with its partner, as per standard practice.

The defects:

  1. Both registered owners must sign. The summary does not confirm that A and B, or the survivor, can convey; if one has died, survivorship may apply and must be documented.
  2. “To be discharged at closing” with no mechanism. Who obtains the discharge, from which lender, and what if it is not delivered?
  3. A “minor” utility easement, undefined. No width, no location, no statement of whether anything may be built over it. Plot it on the plan before calling it minor.
  4. No survey because insurance was ordered. Policies commonly exclude what a survey would show, so skipping it narrows the cover.
  5. A three-week-old search. No bring-down search before funding, so anything registered since will be missed.
  6. Off-register searches not mentioned. No taxes, municipal orders or occupiers’ rights checked.
  7. Joint tenancy for the buyer “as per standard practice.” The co-ownership form is an estate decision. For business partners, survivorship may hand one partner’s share to the other; choose deliberately.

Boardroom drill

Explain this week to a board in two minutes. Set a timer, speak, then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: “When we buy land we buy a bundle of rights, in a particular form of ownership, with other people’s rights on top: mortgages, liens, covenants and easements, many of which bind every future owner. We read the title, the survey and the zoning together before the deposit goes hard, and plot every easement on the plan. We price known problems into the land, insure only unknown defects, and read the policy’s exceptions. We know how the register works in each jurisdiction and run a bring-down search on closing day; if something new appears, we close with a holdback or not at all. In condominiums, the ownership structure puts repairs on the owners, so from Champlain Towers South we take Rule 30: we read who must repair the shared structure, how the money is reserved and what has been reported but not fixed, and we fund the reserve from a professional study from day one.”

How to score your boardroom drill

Listen back for five things. Did you open with the bundle of rights? Did you name at least three kinds of encumbrance? Did you say what title insurance excludes? Did you mention the bring-down search and the holdback? And did you state Rule 30 with care for the case behind it? Score one point for each. Four or five means the week is yours; three or fewer, replay Days 3 and 4.

One exercise for this week

If you own any property, find its title file and check three things: how it is held, every registered encumbrance and whether you have a current survey. If you do not, read the publicly available description of how land registration works in one jurisdiction you might build in, and write down in one paragraph whether it is a registry or a title registration system, and what the state guarantees.

Mistakes to listen for

Listen for three slips. Saying title insurance means you do not need to read the title: it covers the unknown, not the known. Saying an easement is just a line on a plan: it is someone else’s right in your land, binding you and your buyers. And speaking about Champlain Towers South as a story about one board’s mistakes: the lesson is about how a structure of ownership and funding makes delay likely, which is why a developer can design against it.

And a check on composure. This week includes a case in which many people died. If you speak about it in a boardroom, slow down, name the loss plainly and move to the lesson without drama. Respect for the facts is part of being credible about them.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is reading title as a formality handled by lawyers at the end. It is part of the value, decided at the start.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner asks whether title is clean. The professional asks what is on it, what is off it, what each item does to the plan, and who pays to remove it.

Callback

In Week 29 you met the shared facilities agreement in a mixed-use building. This week showed how it binds future owners: it is registered against title, usually as easements and covenants, which is why a mixed-use building’s legal structure has to be designed with its physical one.

head: The six questions
speak: This week I learned that land is a bundle of rights, held in a form of ownership that decides what I can do and who inherits. Joint tenancy passes a share to the survivors; tenancy in common passes it under each owner’s will. Every parcel carries encumbrances: mortgages, liens, covenants and easements, and many bind every future owner. Title problems cost buildable value, time and, in condominiums, special assessments. Title insurance covers some unknown defects but excludes what I know, what a survey would show and much of zoning. Registers either record documents or record title itself, priority usually follows registration, and some rights never appear on title, so I run a bring-down search and close over anything new only with a holdback. Champlain Towers South gave me Rule 30: know who must repair a shared structure, how the money is reserved and what is reported but not fixed.
terms: Restrictive covenant — a registered promise limiting how land may be used or built on, often binding future owners.
Off-register risk — a right or claim that can affect land without appearing on the title register.
Title opinion — a lawyer’s written report on who owns land and what interests and defects affect it.

hostile.q: Your title summary calls the utility easement minor. Where exactly is it, and can you build over it?
hostile.a: It is 3 metres wide along the rear boundary, plotted on the survey and the site plan. The registered instrument prohibits permanent structures within it, so the design keeps the building and the parking deck outside it. Our counsel’s opinion confirms both points in writing.
